problem: Mapless DRL navigation for warehouse docking (driving an AGV underneath a dolly) suffers from sparse positive samples, partial observability from a frontal camera, long training cycles, and the need for precise low-level steering. Map-based pipelines also need localization, mapping and dolly detection, and work only when the dolly is visible.
motivation: Warehouse environments are non-stationary, so building and updating maps is costly, and a learned policy mapping raw multi-modal sensing to continuous control could avoid this. A constricted goal (dolly only 21 cm wider than the vehicle) makes random exploration rarely succeed, so a curriculum over start states is needed to obtain positive experience.
key_idea: Combine distributed Soft Actor-Critic with NavACL-Q, an automatic curriculum that uses a success-prediction network taking geometric properties plus the critic's initial Q-value to pick easy/frontier/random start poses, together with a pre-trained autoencoder feature extractor.
insight: The ablations show both parts matter. NavACL-Q raises the training success (RND averages about 50% with high variance vs >90% for NavACL-Q p.t.) and mean test success (56.6% vs 45.4%). The pre-trained frozen encoder matters even more: the end-to-end variant stagnates around 30% training success even at 0.4M episodes and is 31% lower on average in test. Policies generalise well to interpolated initial orientations (0, ±45°, ±90°) but fail on extrapolated ones (±135°, 180°) not seen in training, so the training domain should match the target domain.
method: Distributed SAC: 9 asynchronous worker environments send episodes to a master that trains the actor and critics using PER, double Q, and auto-tuned temperature
Observation and network: 4 stacked 80x80 RGB frames, current 256-d LiDAR, and last 4 actions and rewards; ResNet-style conv encoder plus FC branches concatenated as learned sensor fusion
Reward design: -0.1 per step, -0.1 dolly collision, -10 other collision, -0.05 for driving slowly, +10 for docking; needs no map so is usable in the real world

NavACL-Q: success-prediction net f_pi (2x32 MLP) takes agent-goal distance, agent clearance, goal clearance, relative angle and the critic's initial Q-value; adaptive filtering samples easy/frontier/random tasks
AF fix: an extra threshold chi=0.95 and a fallback to f>mu_f for easy tasks when mu_f+beta*sigma_f>1, avoiding undersampling of easy tasks
Pre-trained encoder: autoencoder trained with L2 pixel loss on 4-frame stacks from 50k random interaction sequences; encoder weights frozen during RL
Domain randomization: light, texture, obstacles (1-4), and dolly and robot pose across 9 arena cells

setting.backbone: Distributed SAC with ResNet-block conv encoder (autoencoder-pretrained, frozen) + MLPs, trained from scratch by RL
setting.training_data: Online RL interaction in Isaac Sim: about 0.25M episodes / 5M frames (~28 h on 3 GPUs) per run, 3 runs; autoencoder pre-trained on 50,000 random interaction sequences
setting.observation: Frontal 80x80 RGB (4 stacked frames) + two 128-beam LiDARs (256 values) + last 4 actions/rewards; no pose or map
setting.action_space: continuous differential-drive velocities [v, omega], v in [-1,1] m/s, omega in [-1,1] rad/s, 180 ms per action
setting.privileged: none at test time for the DRL agent (privileged goal-distance/angle properties used only for the training curriculum); the baseline uses a global map and dolly pose estimation

numbers.eval_set_note: 11x11 grid of start positions in an unseen arena, 8 orientations, 9 runs each (8712 runs per variant)
numbers.backbone: Distributed SAC + NavACL-Q + pre-trained frozen encoder
numbers.extra: Trained on initial orientations of [-90°,90°]; test includes extrapolated orientations
numbers.evidence: Table validation_stat: average success rate; mean of all relative orientations 56.6 %

numbers.extra: random initial poses instead of curriculum

numbers.backbone: Distributed SAC + NavACL-Q, encoder trained end-to-end

numbers.eval_set_note: same grid test; baseline only feasible when the dolly is visible
numbers.method: NVIDIA Isaac map-based baseline (not the paper's own method)
numbers.backbone: DetectNetv2 + PoseCNN + LQR with map localization
numbers.extra: Uses global map and 720x1280 camera; kept as reference row

numbers_note: No standard benchmark; results are on the authors' own Isaac Sim docking task. Training-curve results (final training success >90% for NavACL-Q p.t.) are given only in figures. The last row is the baseline, included for reference only.
results: NavACL-Q p.t. reaches about 90% test success for four of five interpolated orientations and a mean of 56.6% over all orientations, vs 45.4% for random starts, 25.0% for end-to-end encoder, and 3.1% for NVIDIA's map-based baseline. Performance collapses on extrapolated orientations (±135°, 180°) due to partial observability.
limitations: Poor generalization to initial orientations and distances outside the training range (e.g. +90°, ±135°, 180°, >10 m) because of partial observability with only 4-frame stacking
NavACL-Q fails when early success is too rare for the success network to separate easy from frontier tasks, and still uses domain-specific geometric features
Simulation only, with a frozen pre-trained encoder that breaks fully end-to-end learning; the baseline comparison is limited to visible-dolly cases
compares_to: NVIDIA Isaac SDK map-based pipeline (DetectNetv2 + PoseCNN + LQR)
